# Opening Files {#sec-open-files}

Most projects start the same way: you have a spreadsheet, and you need R to read it. This chapter covers the most common case, a plain `.csv` file — and this time you will do it twice: once by writing the code yourself, and once by clicking through RStudio's menu.

## Our practice dataset

Throughout this book we will use a small, fictional dataset called `diet_habits.csv` — 40 participants, 5 columns, nothing complicated. It's a simplified stand-in for the kind of nutritional epidemiology data you'll actually work with, without the size or complexity of a real study. Download it here: [`diet_habits.csv`](data/diet_habits.csv).

| Column | What it means | Type |
|---|---|---|
| `participant_id` | A number identifying each participant | Identifier |
| `age` | Age in years | Continuous |
| `diet_type` | The dominant diet pattern the participant reports following | Categorical |
| `bmi` | Body Mass Index (kg/m²) | Continuous |
| `daily_calories` | Estimated average daily caloric intake (kcal) | Continuous |

Save this file inside a `data/` folder in your project — the same folder structure we set up in @sec-folders.

## Reading a file with code

```r
survey <- read.csv("data/diet_habits.csv")
head(survey)
```

The arrow `<-` means "store this on the left." This line reads: *read the file, and save the result into an object called `survey`.* From now on, typing `survey` shows you the data, and `head(survey)` shows just the first six rows.

![The console after running the two lines above: `survey` appears in the Environment pane (top-right), and `head(survey)` prints the first six rows below your code.](figures/03-import-menu.png){#fig-import-menu}

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to look for in @fig-console-read
Two things confirm it worked: (1) `survey` shows up in the **Environment** pane, top-right, with "40 obs. of 5 variables" next to it; (2) the printed table below your code has the same 5 column names as the table above. If either is missing, check that `data/diet_habits.csv` is spelled exactly right and sits in the right folder.
:::

## Reading a file with the Import Dataset button

RStudio also offers a point-and-click route, which quietly writes the same code above for you. This is the easiest way to open a file the very first time, before you're comfortable typing `read.csv()` from memory.

**Step 1 — open the menu.**

![File menu → Import Dataset → From Text (readr).](figures/03-import-menu.png){#fig-import-menu}

**Step 2 — browse to `diet_habits.csv` and preview it.**

![The Import dataset window: the preview table on top, the automatically generated code at the bottom. Circled in red: the "Import" button you need to click.](figures/03-import-preview.png){#fig-import-preview}

**Step 3 — watch the console.**

![After clicking Import, RStudio pastes the exact `read_csv(...)` line it used into your console — circled here. Copy this line into your script so the import is reproducible next time.](figures/03-import-console-output.png){#fig-import-console}

::: {.callout-tip}
This is a good way to learn the code by watching the point-and-click path generate it: do it once through the menu, copy the line RStudio prints for you, then paste that line into your `.qmd` or `.R` script so it re-runs automatically next time.
:::

## Common file types

| File extension | Function |
|---|---|
| `.csv` | `read.csv()` |
| `.xlsx` | `readxl::read_excel()` |
| `.txt` (tab-separated) | `read.delim()` |
| `.rds` (R's own format) | `readRDS()` |

::: {.callout-note}
